newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bund futures steady, but underperform.
newsitem.headline: Bund futures steady, but underperform.

text.p: German Bund futures were little changed in late dealings, but continued to lag behind other bond markets as traders grew nervous about the German market's recent fast gains.

Bunds were supported much of the day by strong markets in the U.S. and high yielding countries as well as follow-through buying on the long end of the curve from the Bundesbank's decision not to issue 10-year Bunds in the fourth quarter.
The DTB December Bund future contract was down eight basis points late in the day to 98.80, but well off the high of 99.02.
"The trouble is that we have gone so far already," said Stuart Trow, bond analyst at Norinchukin International Plc. "We will probably trade in a range until spiking out of it."

He and others said although Bunds have climbed, they have not kept up with other markets. High yielding countries, for example, have climbed on increasing optimism about EMU. But Bunds, which already enjoy a stable inflation environment, are less enthusiastic about EMU.
The yield curve flattened somewhat during the day with 10-year maturities in favour after the Bundesbank said Thursday that it would not issue 10-year debt in the fourth quarter.
A surprisingly large drop in VDMA machinery orders of 18 percent in August reinforced the view held by some that the economy here will not pick up steam as quickly as hoped.
Traders said it will be difficult for the contract to climb above important psychological resistance at 99.0, although some see the future contract targeting 100.0.
Traders said they will be keeping a close eye on minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee meeting in August which is scheduled to be released around 2030 GMT.
U.S. unemployment data is likely to be the key focus next week, due at 1230 GMT on Friday, although the NAPM report at 1400 GMT on Tuesday should also get some attention.
Leading finance and monetary officials meeting in Washington this weekend at the International Monetary Fund may also roil markets.
Pro-EMU comments from the likes of Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer could give high-yielding bonds and lift and pull Bunds higher. --Frankfurt Newsroom +49 69 756525
